You win a hand when every other player folds, or by having the strongest five-card hand among players who reach the showdown. A tied best hand can share the pot. You do not have to bet on every turn to keep playing; the guided hand below explains the actions. A standard deck has 52 different cards: thirteen ranks in each of four suits. The usual high-to-low rank order is A K Q J T 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 . A is ace, K king, Q queen, J jack and T ten. The four suits are spades ♠, hearts ♥, diamonds ♦ and clubs ♣. Suits do not outrank one another. You receive two private cards . The shared board arrives as three cards on the flop, one on the turn, then one on the river. Once all five shared cards are out, choose the strongest five from your seven available cards. Use zero, one or two private cards. An ace can be low in A-2-3-4-5, but a straight cannot wrap through K-A-2-3-4.

This is one route through standard 52-card no-limit Texas hold’em: actions and cards, preflop context, the flop, the river, ranges, then betting purpose. Each lesson begins with a limited first pass. Read those sections, explain the check below without the answer, then use a fresh situation to see what needs repair. The longer examples remain available as references. Use a deck, counters or paper. No wager, playing account or purchase is needed. When the cards themselves are unfamiliar, begin with card basics and the best-five hand lab above, then take stage 1. You can pause anywhere or try the checkpoint first when you already know the mechanics. Need smaller steps? The beginner practice room pairs six short worked examples with 18 changed questions. Start with one skill; use mixed practice later to choose what to revisit. Need to practice what happens next at the table? Rehearse one betting round : take each seat’s turn, enter extra counters and follow a line of your own. Cards, actions and the pot Learn: read your two cards, distinguish checking from calling, find the player whose turn it is and compare the best five cards. The lesson finishes with a complete hand whose chips reconcile. Before moving on: explain what you owe now, rather than repeating the last number announced. Use only your contribution on this betting round when counting a call. Your starting hand in context Learn: describe position, earlier action, effective stacks and the price before asking whether two cards are worth playing. A hand's label leaves out most of the decision. Before moving on: distinguish information you observed from an assumption about hidden cards. Name who still has a turn, including a player who may raise after your call. Your first decisions after the flop Learn: name the made hand and the draw separately, read checks and raises without inventing the opponent's cards, and notice when a helpful shared card improves the other hand too. Before moving on: explain both what your cards make now and what they still need. A possibility to improve is different from a completed hand or a guaranteed win. The turn, river and showdown Learn: rebuild the hand when a new card arrives, recognize that a missed draw can still have showdown value, and distinguish calling a bluff from making one. On the river there is no further community card to rescue a draw. Before moving on: separate the price of a call from evidence that your hand meets it. Say when the action is complete and whether you are counting outright wins or a share of the pot. Your first range Learn: separate known cards, physically possible hands and assumptions about their frequency. You do not need a chart or percentages for the first pass. Before moving on: name a fact and an assumption separately. A check is an observed action; the opponent’s hidden hand remains unknown. Betting with a purpose Learn: name which worse hands might call a value bet or which better hands might fold to a bluff. Compare a bet with checking when nothing is owed. Before moving on: describe the response you need, rather than using “I have a pair” or “I won the pot” as the whole argument. Keep your place without another account. The five tasks below are a menu for later study. They are not another beginner course to finish, and the external course is optional. Work at your own pace. A session can be split across several days, repeated, or skipped when you can already do its task. Use a deck on a table, a fictional example or a completed hand. None of these activities requires a wager. Keep two headings in your notes: “What I can now explain” and “What I still need to check.” Those notes are more informative than the number of pages opened. The linked external pages are free to read as listed, although their publishers may also sell products or advertise gambling. 1. Tell the story of one hand. Read one hand from deal to showdown . Then close the page and describe the order: private cards, preflop betting, flop, turn, river and showdown if more than one player remains. Name who still has a decision at each step. Use the official hold'em rules and hand-rankings references below when you get stuck. Your output is a short explanation of a single hand, not a memorized glossary. Before moving on, explain why a hand can finish without anyone showing cards and why winning a pot does not equal gaining that whole amount in profit. 2. Reconstruct a small pot. Use bets, calls and side pots , then write the separate contributions in a fictional heads-up river example. There are 60 chips in the pot before an opponent bets 30. Calling costs another 30, making the final pot 120. With no further betting or fees and ordinary showdown equity, the break-even share is 30 / 120 = 25% . Your task is to label the 60, the opponent's 30 and your additional 30. Do not divide by 90 simply because that is what you can see before calling. The free expected-value article below offers a second explanation. For a longer worked exercise, use the pot-odds workshop . 3. Explain a decision before seeing the ending. Open the river Decision Lab . Before opening the answer panels, write the cost of calling and the assumption about the opponent that would matter most. Then inspect the two endings. Your output is one explanation that distinguishes the decision from its result. You do not have to guess the best action. Finding the missing information is useful. “The opponent could have a bluff” is a possibility, not a measurement of how frequently that opponent bluffs. 4. Choose the kind of poker you want to understand. For live tournaments, use the field guide and identify three event details to confirm. For cash games, read the cash-game study guide and name the relevant costs. For Omaha or a mixed-game broadcast, use the game comparison before judging a showdown. Your output is a statement of the game, betting structure and question. An introductory hold'em rule is not a universal instruction for every game with poker chips. 5. Study one lesson, not an entire archive. MIT's 2016 course page below provides a free university course with video lectures. It is historical teaching material, not a current commercial solver manual. Choose one lesson relevant to your question and note the assumptions behind its examples. The site listing does not mean every video has been watched or every claim independently reproduced. Finish with three sentences: the question, what the lesson helped clarify, and what it did not establish. Keep the next step small using the resource-check sheet . When the lesson is too advanced, return to the specific missing concept instead of concluding you need a more expensive course.

    Five actions, in plain language
    Check
    Add nothing when you owe nothing. Keep your hand.

    Open wagering on a postflop round. Here the opening bet is at least 2, the big blind.

    Increase the total wager by at least the last full bet or raise. The big blind is a live wager before the flop.
    Fold
    Give up the hand when facing a wager. Earlier payments stay in the pot. Use checking when you owe nothing in this exercise; folding when not facing a wager can violate live tournament procedure.
